title: The Open Boat
text:
Stephen Crane based this story on his own experience. In January 1897 the steamer he was on sank off the coast of Florida, and he spent more than a day in a small dinghy before reaching shore.

In the story, four men were left in a ten-foot boat on a rough sea after their ship went down: the injured captain, the cook, the oiler Billie, and a newspaper correspondent. The waves were so steep that every one of them threatened to swamp the boat. The cook bailed. The captain, unable to row, gave orders and kept their spirits up. The oiler and the correspondent took turns at the oars, changing places carefully so as not to tip the boat, rowing until they could hardly move.

They could see the shore and a lighthouse, but no one saw them, and the surf was too heavy to land. They spent a long night at sea, taking turns to row and sleep. Crane wrote that among the four grew a subtle brotherhood, a comradeship the correspondent felt was the best experience of his life.

The next morning they decided to take the boat through the surf. It overturned, and they swam for the beach. Rescuers on shore pulled the captain, the cook and the correspondent out alive. The oiler, the strongest of them, who had rowed the hardest, was found dead on the sand.
lesson: Shared danger can forge a deep bond in people who would otherwise have little in common. In a crisis, take turns, share the load, and keep each other going.
people: The captain, the cook, Billie the oiler, the correspondent
location: Off the coast of Florida, USA
